impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's application of its Penumbra framework—rather than the Federal Circuit's Dynamic Drinkware written description analysis—to determine when a reference patent qualifies as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2) based on a provisional application's filing date was correct.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's finding that claims of the '409 patent were unpatentable as obvious, holding that the Board needed to reconsider whether a key prior art reference (Carrier) was entitled to the filing date of its provisional application under AIA § 102(d)(2). The court questioned the Board's Penumbra framework, which applied a lower standard than Dynamic Drinkware's written description requirement for establishing prior art dates. This decision has significant implications for how provisional application filing dates are used to establish prior art status in IPR proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from a potentially higher bar for challengers seeking to use provisional application dates to establish prior art, making it harder to invalidate patents in IPR proceedings based on references with thin provisional support.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies challenging patents in IPR proceedings face greater uncertainty and potentially higher burdens when relying on reference patents whose prior art status depends on provisional application filing dates.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 applies differently to method claims (such as methods of treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies) than to composition claims, and whether broad functional method claims are adequately enabled.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache using anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies against an enablement challenge. Judge Dyk's dissent argued the panel's holding creates confusion about enablement standards for method claims and will sustain overly broad claims that undermine medical innovation, contrary to the Supreme Court's Amgen precedent. The denial preserves a potentially more lenient enablement standard for method claims compared to genus composition claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims benefit from a more permissive enablement standard, allowing broader patent protection for therapeutic methods even where the full scope of functional antibody genus claims may not be fully enabled.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech competitors face broader blocking patents on therapeutic methods, potentially limiting freedom to develop alternative antibody-based treatments within broadly claimed functional genera.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether functionality determinations in design patent claim construction present factual questions for the jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a design patent infringement case, with a sharp split among the judges. The concurrence defended the Egyptian Goddess ordinary observer test as properly allowing summary judgment when designs are sufficiently distinct, while the dissent (joined by four judges) argued the framework has been misapplied to focus on dissimilarity and that functionality questions in design patent claim construction should go to the jury. The denial preserves the current approach but signals deep division on design patent infringement standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the continued ability to obtain summary judgment of non-infringement when designs are sufficiently distinct, reducing litigation costs in design patent cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face a framework that may favor finding non-infringement at summary judgment by focusing on differences, and the denial of en banc review leaves unresolved concerns about jury trial rights on functionality issues in claim construction.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the licensed patents such that the licensee could sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the license had automatically terminated when the licensee shifted its business to enforcement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue for infringement in its own name without joining A&M. The court also held that the licensee had not ceased business operations merely by shifting to patent enforcement activities, so the license had not automatically terminated. This decision provides important guidance on the sufficiency of exclusive license agreements for patent standing purposes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent enforcement entities benefit from clearer standards confirming that comprehensive exclusive licenses can convey sufficient rights to sue independently, and that shifting to enforcement-focused business models does not trigger automatic license termination.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential defense strategy of challenging patent enforcement entities' standing based on the argument that the patent owner must be joined or that the license terminated when the entity shifted to enforcement.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert testimony and in setting aside the jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two damages models it had previously excluded. The court also reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury award, while affirming the denial of Ford's motion for judgment as a matter of law on trade secret misappropriation liability. This decision is significant for how courts evaluate damages models in complex trade secret cases involving software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret owners benefit from broader latitude in presenting damages models, as the Federal Circuit required the district court to reconsider excluded damages theories, and the reinstatement of the jury's breach of contract award protects IP licensors' contractual expectations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop in-house replacements for licensed software face sustained trade secret misappropriation liability, and the remand for reconsideration of damages models creates continued exposure to potentially larger damages awards.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a split decision on patent eligibility under § 101, vacating summary judgment of eligibility for claims of two patents while affirming eligibility for claims of two other patents. The court also affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages. The decision provides important guidance on the Alice/Mayo framework as applied to communications technology patents, distinguishing between claims that recite abstract mathematical concepts and those directed to specific technological improvements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology benefit from the court's affirmance that claims directed to specific non-uniform constellation designs with concrete technological improvements can survive § 101 challenges, supporting patent value in standards-related technologies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing communications standards face continued patent infringement risk, and the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty about the scope of patent-eligible subject matter for signal processing innovations that involve mathematical optimization.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a communications apparatus with a coupler matching transmitter impedance to the characteristic impedance of air are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), even though the district court found them indefinite.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds. The court held that while the claims were sufficiently definite, they were invalid for lack of enablement because the specification did not enable the full scope of the claimed invention. This decision demonstrates the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds and reinforces the enablement requirement as a meaningful constraint on patent scope.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds not relied upon by the district court, providing additional defensive options even when primary invalidity theories fail.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face risk that claims surviving one invalidity challenge may still be invalidated on alternative grounds raised by defendants, requiring robust specification support across all potential invalidity theories.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations under 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling based on the pendency of a prior class action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, affirming dismissal of claims by bank investors who lost assets during the 2008 financial crisis. The court recognized that its prior decision in Bright v. United States has been implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's ANZ Securities decision, which held that statutory filing deadlines not subject to equitable tolling are also not subject to American Pipe tolling. This decision eliminates American Pipe tolling as a tool for claimants in the Court of Federal Claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: The federal government benefits from a firm six-year statute of limitations in Tucker Act cases that cannot be extended by the pendency of class actions, providing greater certainty and finality against stale claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Businesses and individuals with claims against the federal government in the Court of Federal Claims lose the ability to rely on American Pipe tolling from prior class actions, requiring independent timely filing of individual claims within the six-year limitations period.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly dismissed a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, awarded attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and sanctioned plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 for filing a frivolous patent infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal without leave to amend and the fee award, finding the case exceptional under § 285 where the plaintiff filed suit seeking pre-suit damages without adequate basis. The court addressed the enforceability of attorney fee awards and sanctions against both the patent assertion entity and its counsel. This decision reinforces the consequences of pursuing meritless patent infringement claims and the availability of fee-shifting under § 285.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from strong precedent supporting fee-shifting and sanctions against patent plaintiffs and their counsel who file inadequately supported infringement claims, deterring frivolous patent litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and their counsel face heightened risk of fee-shifting and personal sanctions when bringing infringement claims without adequate pre-filing investigation, particularly when seeking pre-suit damages.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient analysis in denying a defendant's motions for Rule 11 sanctions and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 where the plaintiff's patent had claims similar to related patents that received § 101 rejections from the PTO.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and fees, finding the order provided insufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent holder who filed suit after the PTO had rejected claims in related patent applications under § 101, and after a related patent had been found ineligible in separate litigation. The decision emphasizes that district courts must articulate adequate reasoning when deciding fee and sanctions motions in patent cases involving questionable assertions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers gain stronger appellate tools to challenge denials of fee awards where patent holders pursue litigation despite significant indicators of invalidity, encouraging more thorough judicial analysis of exceptional case determinations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased risk that filing suit with patents related to those previously found ineligible or rejected under § 101 may result in fee-shifting and sanctions if the district court's reasoning is required to be more transparent.

impacts.caseName: Socket Solutions, LLC v. Import Global, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in granting a preliminary injunction barring the sale of an accused product based on a patent covering electrical wall outlet covers.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the preliminary injunction against Import Global's Neat Socket product and remanded for further proceedings, finding deficiencies in the district court's analysis. The decision addresses the standards for preliminary injunctions in patent cases, including the requirements for demonstrating likelihood of success on the merits and irreparable harm. This ruling is significant for consumer product companies facing or seeking preliminary injunctive relief in patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the Federal Circuit's rigorous review of preliminary injunction standards, providing protection against premature market exclusion based on insufficiently supported infringement theories.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders seeking preliminary injunctions face a high bar for demonstrating entitlement to pre-trial relief, even where the accused product appears to closely replicate the patented invention.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of invalidity by anticipation and non-infringement of patents directed to drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants used in coronary stent systems.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict finding infringement and willfulness, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to JMOL of both invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement. The court found that prior art anticipated the asserted claims and that BSC's drug-eluting stent products did not infringe. This decision overturns a significant damages award and has implications for medical device patent litigation involving drug-eluting stent technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device manufacturers benefit from the reversal of a patent infringement verdict, confirming that well-established prior art in the drug-eluting stent field can invalidate university-held patents and that careful claim construction can defeat infringement theories.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent holders and research institutions face the risk that commercialized medical device patents may be found anticipated by prior art, undermining licensing revenue streams from industry partnerships.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement case on both improper venue under 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b) and failure to state a claim under § 101 patent eligibility grounds simultaneously, or must limit itself to venue dismissal alone.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dual dismissal on both improper venue and § 101 patent ineligibility grounds, rejecting the plaintiff's argument that the court should have stopped after finding venue improper. The court held that the e-commerce 'bridge computer' patent claims were ineligible under § 101. This decision confirms that district courts may address patent eligibility even when venue is independently grounds for dismissal, providing res judicata-like protection against serial filings in different venues.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability of district courts to resolve § 101 eligibility alongside venue challenges, preventing patent holders from simply refiling in proper venues after venue dismissals and forcing repeated defense costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities lose the ability to treat venue dismissals as opportunities to refile in more favorable jurisdictions, as district courts can simultaneously adjudicate patent eligibility on the merits.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement's contingent payment provision tied to the outcome of an ex parte reexamination.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a contract dispute between T-Mobile and KAIFI regarding whether the phrase 'survives the EPR' in their settlement agreement triggered a contingent payment obligation, because the dispute was a state law contract interpretation question that did not necessarily depend on resolving a substantial patent law question. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This decision clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for settlement agreement disputes arising from patent litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies involved in patent settlement agreements benefit from clarity that contractual interpretation disputes will be resolved by regional circuits applying relevant state law, potentially leading to more predictable contract interpretation frameworks.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties drafting patent litigation settlement agreements face risk that disputes over patent-related contingent payment provisions may be litigated in regional circuits rather than the Federal Circuit, losing the specialized patent court's expertise and potentially facing different interpretive approaches.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims to crystalline forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate salt, pharmaceutical formulations thereof, and methods of treating cancer therewith satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that Exelixis's Malate Salt Patents had adequate written description, upholding the validity of claims covering crystalline cabozantinib (L)-malate — the active ingredient in the cancer drug Cabometyx®. The decision is significant for pharmaceutical patent holders defending polymorph and salt-form patents against generic challengers, confirming that specifications describing both crystalline and amorphous forms with preparation examples can satisfy written description for claims to specific crystalline forms.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance that polymorph and crystalline salt patents with detailed specification examples satisfy written description, protecting valuable drug products like Cabometyx® from generic competition through 2030.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers face continued market exclusion from patented crystalline drug forms, as the decision reinforces the validity of formulation patents that may extend protection beyond the original compound patent expiration.
